La Converse s’est entretenue avec des él: La Converse spoke with voters from Latin American communities to find out what concerns the Spanish-speaking Latino electorate.
En tant qu’immigrante hispanique d’origi: As a Hispanic immigrant of Latin American origin, I closely followed last year’s U.S. presidential election and the role voters from our communities played in that process.
Lorsque des élections ont été annoncées: When an election was called in Canada, the first question that came to mind was: how will the country’s Hispanic Latinos vote?
Bien sûr, les contextes ne sont pas les: Of course, the contexts are not the same. For one thing, we have two different political systems, and for another, Hispanics make up a very small share of Canada’s population – we don’t carry the same weight as the Hispanic community does in the American electorate.
Je me suis aussi demandé quelles étaient: I also wondered what the main concerns of the Latin American electorate in Canada were, particularly in light of the U.S. government’s recent economic measures and its stated intention to annex the country.
J’ai fait plusieurs constats intéressant: I came away with several interesting findings. First, many Latinos are afraid to openly express their political views or to be associated with any particular leaning. Second, those who are sure of their vote are mobilizing to get more voters out to the polls. Third, what is happening in the United States is one of the reasons many people are taking part in this election, either because they believe Canada and its sovereignty must be protected, or because they think it could be an opportunity to build closer ties with the United States.
Lundi, je suis allée voter par anticipat: On Monday, I went to vote in the advance polls. I have done so in previous elections, at every level of government, and I can say without a doubt that this is the time I have seen the most people lining up to drop their ballot in the box.
En tant que Vénézuélienne vivant à l’étr: As a Venezuelan living abroad, I can say that taking part in elections in my country is a right that was ripped away from me. That is why I consider that voting in a democracy is not only a privilege, but also a civic duty.
Je n’aurais jamais pensé prendre part à: I never thought I would take part in such an exciting – and such a worrying – election in my host country. But here we are.

Aurora Pacheco pourra voter pour la prem: Aurora Pacheco will vote for the first time in next week’s federal election. The 44-year-old Venezuelan became a Canadian citizen in 2024. Besides voting for the Liberal Party, she decided to sign up as a volunteer at the party’s office in LaSalle, in Montréal. “It feels good to actively represent the Latin American community and to help my friends understand the importance of voting, because today more than ever, we need it.”
Lorsque nous lui parlons au téléphone, A: When we speak with her by phone, Aurora is enthusiastic and highly motivated by the idea of taking part in the electoral process. For her, voting in Canada is a great opportunity and a privilege she intends to make the most of. “Here, we can speak freely without fear. We can learn about the different platforms. The vote will be respected. The parties that don’t win will be in opposition. That is vital to the health of a government.”
Au-delà des sondages, Aurora s’inquiète: Beyond the polls, Aurora is worried about the narrow margins separating the two main parties. “I know people who are voting Conservative because they’re fed up with Trudeau. There are also a lot of Venezuelans voting Conservative just because Poilievre’s wife is Venezuelan, and I wonder how a Poilievre victory is going to benefit us, the Venezuelans.”
Comme Aurora, 3,3 % de la population can: Like Aurora, 3.3% of the Canadian population – of Latin American origin – will be able to express – or not – its interest in national politics on April 28.
Aucune étude n’a cependant été consacrée: However, no study has been devoted to the voting behaviour of Hispanic Latinos in Canadian elections. According to Statistics Canada figures, though, we do know that naturalized Canadian citizens vote more when they have been in the country for a long time. The turnout rate is 71% among citizens who have lived in the country for more than 10 years. In addition, according to Elections Canada, the group of citizens originally from Central America, South America and the Caribbean recorded a turnout rate of 73.3% in the 2000 federal election.
Vingt-cinq ans plus tard, trois grands s: Twenty-five years later, three major issues are driving voters of Hispanic American origin to take part in the federal election: the economy, potential changes to immigration policies, and the influence of the U.S. government on domestic affairs.
D’origine argentine, Victor Armony, prof: Victor Armony, who is of Argentine origin and a professor in the Department of Sociology at UQAM, has done research on immigrant populations, focusing in particular on Latin American communities in Canada. According to him, “the little information we have suggests that Latinos tend to participate in elections. We can partly see it in the nominations. Today, we see people of Latin American origin at every level of government: in municipalities, such as Montréal, in Quebec provincial politics and in the federal Parliament. Until Prime Minister Justin Trudeau resigned, two of his ministers were people born in Latin America: Pablo Rodríguez, the Minister of Transport, who is of Argentine origin, and Soraya Martínez, the Minister of Tourism, who is of Chilean origin.”
Même s’il n’y a pas beaucoup de députés: Even though there are not many MPs originally from Latin America, Victor Armony stresses one important point: “We must not forget that people from Latin American immigrant backgrounds make up no more than 3% of the Canadian population. So I would say that the representation is quite significant.”
L’expert souligne en effet que « les soc: The expert points out that “Latin American societies are highly politicized, which perhaps shows in the behaviour of the members of their diasporas; not so much in their activism, but in the fact that they stay well informed and go out to vote.” According to Mr. Armony, one of the reasons for this interest is the political experience in their societies of origin, which are unstable and conflict-ridden, and where problems such as inflation, poverty, corruption, insecurity and authoritarianism are common.

Les élections fédérales de 2025 susciten: The 2025 federal election is generating a great deal of interest, but also a certain anxiety, both among Hispanic Latinos who are eligible to vote and among those who cannot yet exercise that right because they have not been naturalized.
Selon M. Armony, cette élection devrait: According to Mr. Armony, this election should see high turnout, “especially if you take into account the mobilization of many Canadians against the tariffs imposed by the U.S. government: cancelling trips to the United States, boycotting American imports, buying local products, and so on. The level of civic motivation is high, which should translate into strong voter turnout.”
Or, précise-t-il, « les Latino-Américain: However, he explains, “Latin Americans particularly appreciate the stability of Canadian society. Economic peace of mind is perhaps the most important aspect, and that is precisely what the U.S. government’s policies are currently putting at risk.”
Cecilia Escamilla connaît bien les commu: Cecilia Escamilla knows the Latin American communities of La Belle Province well, particularly those in Montréal. She heads the Centre d’aide aux familles latino-américaines (CAFLA). A community worker for more than 20 years, she leads this non-profit organization and says she is concerned about the short-term future of Latin American communities.
« Tout d’abord, il y a l’immigration. Je: “First of all, there is immigration. I’m worried about the changes at the federal level and what they mean for asylum seekers, students, and families without papers and without status. These people have access to practically no benefits and are exploited for their labour, which makes them doubly vulnerable,” she explains.
Le deuxième facteur que M<sup>me </sup>E: The second factor that M<sup>s</sup>. Escamilla considers essential in this election is the impact political rhetoric has on fundamental values such as coexistence, acceptance, inclusion, tolerance and respect, particularly toward disadvantaged people.
Elle ajoute avoir été récemment témoin d: She adds that she has recently witnessed episodes of intolerance that lead her to think that “these values have weakened a great deal in this society. That doesn’t help integration at all. It also has significant consequences on the mental health of people from immigrant communities,” she says.
La travailleuse communautaire observe ce: The community worker sees this phenomenon every day: “We’re receiving more and more requests for mental health support services, and we can’t keep up. I’m also very concerned about the cuts that could be made to the various organizations serving communities. I think the effect will be huge, and I’m worried about the future of social organizations. We all have more and more needs and less and less funding,” she stresses.
Jesús Ardila, un Vénézuélien installé au: Jesús Ardila, a Venezuelan who has lived in Canada for 40 years, has always considered himself a centrist. But this time, the pediatrician and father of nine Canadian-born children plans to vote Conservative. “I’m determined to move to the right, and it’s the catastrophe this country is going through that led me to make that decision.”
L’économie et le coût des logements au p: The economy and the cost of housing in the country worry him in particular. “I think Canadians’ quality of life has been sacrificed,” he confides.
Il récuse ce qu’il appelle « le libertin: He rejects what he calls “the libertinism of immigration”: “I believe in the value of immigration, but the government has let in millions of immigrants without considering the services and the quality it can offer to the people already living here. It affects health care, education and basic services, as well as safety.”
Le médecin se plaint également de certai: The doctor also complains about certain ideas that he considers “a consequence of the liberal worldview and wokeism.” He refers in particular to gender diversity. “For me, there are only two sexes: man and woman. In my practice, I have an obligation to provide care, to respect and to treat all patients. However, with so many shortcomings in so many areas, this woke vision only creates more social conflict.”
Il a fait confectionner une casquette gr: He had a cap made emblazoned with the slogan “Make Canada Great Again.” Unsurprisingly, he also says he is a Trump supporter. “A lot of people don’t like the guy because he’s crude, but he’s a negotiator,” he says. The imposition of 25% tariffs on Canada is not a problem for Jesús Ardila, since, he believes, it is “a ploy [by Donald Trump] to relieve the pressure on his country. He’s pressuring Canada to do business with him.” In his view, “all of this will be resolved once we have a new prime minister.”
Selon le médecin, Pierre Poilievre est d: According to the doctor, Pierre Poilievre is therefore the ideal candidate to stand up to Trump. “They’re going to understand each other like two brothers, annoyed and happy. He’s going to work hard with Trump so that we become great again and so that we generate resources.”
Il n’est pas tout à fait convaincu par l: He is not entirely sold on the idea of making Canada the 51<sup>st</sup> state of its neighbour, but he still thinks it makes some sense. “I don’t completely agree, because this country has its history, its bilingualism; but economically, I think Canadian citizens would be better off joining the United States,” he says.
Angel Castilla, un charpentier de constr: Angel Castilla, a 25-year-old Spanish-Venezuelan construction carpenter, will not be able to take part in this election, since he has only lived in Canada for three years. However, he is volunteering for the Conservative Party in Toronto. He was active with the right-wing party Vox in Spain before immigrating to Canada.
« Ici, tout allait bien : c’était une so: “Everything was going well here: it was an incredible society, where you worked, where you saved, and where you got everything you wanted. You could buy a car, save for a house, and much more. But since I arrived, I’ve seen a brutal decline in the economic and social aspects,” he says.
L’administration libérale n’a pas bien f: The Liberal administration hasn’t done things right and has stayed in power too long, he believes. He thinks young people like him, even if they can’t vote, can help with mobilization.
Les bénévoles créent notamment des éléme: Volunteers create, among other things, non-traditional political propaganda. With that in mind, and under the slogan “Bring it Home,” Mr. Castilla and colleagues created a salsa song in English, shared on the channels of the group Latinos4Pierre, of which he is a member.
Le jeune pro-conservateur affirme que «: The young Conservative supporter says that “Liberal governance is based on censoring those who speak out against them.” He cites <l1>Bill C-18</l1> [known as the Online News Act], “which means I can’t even see the news from my own country, because it’s blocked,” he believes.
Il évoque également la <l1>loi C-63</l1>: He also brings up <l1>Bill C-63</l1> [the Online Harms Act], which, according to [the Liberals], aims to combat online hate crimes, but which, in his view, is “actually another form of censorship, because when hate is directed at those who don’t think like them, they do nothing,” he notes.
Le jeune homme estime que, dans cette él: The young man believes that freedom, the economy, security and society are at stake in this election. “This administration has led to a lot of spending and massive restrictions on projects that could benefit Canada. International investors are turning away and going to the United States.”
À propos du pays voisin, Angel Castilla: As for the neighbouring country, Angel Castilla doesn’t think Donald Trump’s tariff measures will be a long-term problem either. “Canada’s problem isn’t Trump, it’s the current government. I don’t want a politician who wants to go to economic war, I want a strong politician who looks for a solution. I think Pierre can get a good deal,” he says.
Quant à l’annexion du Canada par les Éta: As for the annexation of Canada by the United States, he doesn’t think it’s serious. “The Trump administration excels at marketing and trolling bad politicians. People are making a big drama out of nonsense, instead of focusing on what really matters,” he adds.
Il est également persuadé que la popular: He is also convinced that Pierre Poilievre’s popularity is far greater than the polls show. “A lot of people are with Pierre. They’re in the workers’ unions. They line up nonstop. It’s happening at the rallies. I think his popularity is bigger than we imagine; it just doesn’t show,” he says.
Même son de cloche du côté d’Isaac Mendo: Isaac Mendoza, a 29-year-old Cuban who has lived in Toronto since 2019, sings the same tune. He will vote Conservative in this election, for the economy and for the possibility of making changes to trade between provinces, “which Pierre Poilievre had promised to take care of.” Over the past 10 years, the Liberals have destroyed the economy and created an almost total dependence on the United States, he says. “It’s easier to trade [from Ontario] with New York than with Alberta,” he laments.
Isaac pense que le parti libéral est au: Isaac thinks the Liberal Party has been in power for too long, and he is not satisfied with its management. He also considers that the party “is closer to communism than to democracy,” and, having lived under a communist dictatorship, “I know first-hand all the disasters and all the suffering it can cause.”
La rue Saint-Hubert, à Montréal, accueil: Rue Saint-Hubert, in Montréal, draws a large number of Hispanics who come from other neighbourhoods to shop there. We spoke with some passersby, but not all of them wanted to share their political opinions. In fact, most of them are wary. They don’t feel comfortable talking, saying whether or not they vote, and are even less inclined to say who they’re voting for. Those who do talk prefer not to be quoted by their last name or photographed.
C’est le cas de Felipe, 55 ans, qui atte: That is the case with Felipe, 55, who is waiting with his dog while his wife finishes shopping. The couple, originally from Mexico, have lived in Montréal for three years and are applying for permanent residence, which prevents them from voting for now. Felipe admits he is not very familiar with the proposals of the various political parties, but says he is very worried about this election and about how the results will affect his life in Canada.
« Je crains qu’un nouveau gouvernement n: “I’m afraid a new government will take harsh measures against immigrants. Every time there’s a change of government, policies change. I know that some people break the law, but not everyone does. Unfortunately, when those changes come, the whole burden falls on those of us who are trying to do our paperwork properly.”
Ana Villanueva, 49 ans, d’origine mexica: Ana Villanueva, 49, who is of Mexican origin, admits for her part that she was afraid the Liberal Party had no chance of winning the election, after the tumultuous days leading up to Justin Trudeau’s departure. So she got involved. “I did something I’d never done before: I joined the party, I donated, I went to a rally and I voted in the leadership race. I think the stakes in this election are high,” she says.
Pour Ana, il est crucial d’inclure dans: For Ana, it is crucial to include on the list of issues “the fact that in the United States, they’re trying to wipe out diversity.” In her view, “it’s more important than ever to have, in Canada, a traditionally inclusive and diverse country, someone who will keep promoting that value. I think Poilievre will be a carbon copy of Trump, and that’s frightening,” she adds.
Elle cite, pêle-mêle, la défense des dro: She cites, in no particular order, the defence of human rights, environmental protection and women’s rights, values with which she thinks the Liberal Party is more aligned.
Bien qu’il soit difficile de déterminer: While it is hard to determine whether the Hispanic Latino electorate in Canada identifies more with one party than another, it is nonetheless clear that it is actively mobilizing and that U.S. influence is a key issue in this community’s mind.
Ce matin, dans la cuisine de la maison,: This morning, in the kitchen at home, my husband and I had the conversation we have every day, a sort of private podcast between two journalists who drink coffee and discuss the news as if it were any other domestic matter. It is more than unusual to interview your spouse, which is why I want to be very transparent about it. But it so happens that my husband, Rafael Osío Cabrices, is a journalist with more than 30 years of experience covering Latin American political and cultural issues and the editor-in-chief of Caracas Chronicles, an English-language Venezuelan media outlet based in the United States.
Selon lui, les Latinos sont en général c: According to him, Latinos are generally conservative by definition, notably because of the influence of the Catholic and evangelical religions. “The Canadian centre and left, the Liberals and the NDP, talk about themes that, in Latin America, are used by the governments that many immigrants fled, and it’s simple arithmetic that pushes them even further to the right.” In effect, some Latin Americans’ votes would be guided by the logic “if I’m against the left in my country of origin, then I’m also against everything the left proposes in my host country.” Issues like LGBTQ+ rights, the environment, abortion and feminism, which are championed in Canada by the centre and the left, are therefore turn-offs for these immigrants. “Latino voters in general are not only hostile to these issues because they don’t understand them well, but also because they associate them – sometimes wrongly – with individuals like Nicolás Maduro (Venezuela), Miguel Díaz Canel (Cuba) and Daniel Ortega (Nicaragua), among others, and that’s a factor that neither the Democrats in the United States nor the Liberals or the NDP here have been able to grasp,” he explains.
Pierre Poilievre, quant à lui, a intégré: Pierre Poilievre, for his part, has incorporated these issues into his message. “I think the alarmism over social issues and the criticism of the Liberals’ economic management are at the heart of the reasons why a good portion of the Hispanic electorate in Canada supports him,” he says.
Il mentionne également les discours cata: He also points to the doom-laden rhetoric, filled with fake news and conspiracy theories, that circulates on social media and WhatsApp.” Yet many Latinos get their information from these platforms. “Poilievre has been benefiting from this rhetoric since the pandemic and the truckers’ convoy crisis in Ottawa, and it has grown much stronger since Trump’s victory,” he adds.
Une question qui a particulièrement rete: One question that caught the attention of many American analysts during Trump’s campaign was why an immigrant electorate could identify with a leader who looks nothing like them. Rafael has an idea: “Some Latinos admire and identify with Trump partly because he’s a millionaire, but mostly because he’s a guy who does what he wants and because he offers simple, immediate solutions to these big problems that, in reality, are nothing more than imaginary problems.” He is referring specifically to ideas that have been fed in the world of fake news.
Rafael estime que des menaces inexistant: Rafael believes that non-existent threats have been created and inflated, and that they fuel homophobia and racism among some immigrants. “No, their children aren’t going to be ‘homosexualized’ in schools, abortion isn’t going to be used as a method of contraception, and the white Western society that Latinos want to fit into isn’t going to be replaced by Muslims, gay people, Black people, and so on.” Trump and Poilievre sold themselves as the easy, simple solution to a great catastrophe that is supposed to happen but that, in reality, doesn’t exist.”
